chapter_theme: The last run of the Valayapathi fragments: a verse against a blind guide to release, then the sequence (49-60) in which an old courtesan gives her daughter ten models, from the river to the chaste wife, and each is glossed as a way of following wealth; gnomic verses on poverty, household virtue and the conditions without which goods are void; and fragments from commentaries, Jain sages and a proud lute master, and two refrains to the heart on the burning of the adorned body and the striving that leads to attainment.

cast.role: the aged dancer-courtesan who instructs her daughter (49-50)
an unnamed player who bows to the Jain sages and sets the story to the lute (67)
an unnamed master of the ninety-six kinds of musical sequence (68)
the speaker's own heart, addressed in the refrains of 70 and 71

48.reading: Someone without sound knowledge who offers to destroy wholly the faults done before and tells the way to blissful release to one who does not know it is like a blind man telling a blind man the road.
48.nuance: The verse names no school and no teacher; whose rival guide is meant belonged to the lost story. முந்துசெய் குற்றம் (faults done before) makes the false teacher's offer a promise to clear past deeds, so the charge is that he lacks the knowledge such clearing needs.

claims.claim: one who lacks true knowledge cannot guide another to release, however much he promises to remove past faults

49.reading: The aged dancer-courtesan tells her daughter to behave like the river, the lute, the fire-drill, the moon, the climbing creeper, the ship, the chaste wife and the beast, and the verse says these are best shown in another place.
49.nuance: Line 4 promises that the comparisons will be opened out elsewhere, and verses 51-60 do so in the order of this list (river 51, lute 52, fire-drill 53, moon 54, creeper 55, ship 56, chaste wife 57, beast 58), with 50's monkey and bee in 59 and 60. The chaste wife stands in a list of things and animals: that placement is the satire.
49.event: An aged dancer-courtesan instructs her daughter to conduct herself like a list of things, among them the chaste wife.

50.reading: Without preface she adds the monkey and the bright-winged bee as models, and the verse seems to say that these too fit those who come trusting the daughter's shoulders and bringing great wealth.
50.nuance: பாயிரம் இன்றி, without preface, may mean she taught bluntly, with no introduction. நின் in line 3 addresses the daughter, so lines 3-4 may still be the mother's words; the syntax of line 4 is hard to fix.
50.event: The old courtesan adds the monkey and the bee to her list of models for her daughter.

51.reading: Courtesans are like a river: their love swells as the inflow of wealth swells and shrinks as it shrinks, as the stream rises with the rain and dries away completely.
51.nuance: வாரி serves twice: the flood of a river and the inflow of income. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

claims.claim: a courtesan's love rises and falls exactly with the lover's wealth

52.reading: Courtesans are like the lute: whoever holds the wealth, their love is suited to him, as a lute plays for whatever bard takes it up.
52.nuance: The repeated எங்ஙனம் ... அங்ஙனம் (however ... so) makes the love a function of the wealth, whatever its source. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

claims.claim: a courtesan's love belongs to whoever holds the wealth, not to a person

53.reading: Courtesans are like the fire-drill: by many arts and devices, once men are in their hands, they draw wealth out of them as the drill-stick turned in the hands draws fire.
53.nuance: The image is friction: the stick yields fire only while it is worked. Line 2 (கரணம் எனும் இலர்) and line 3's word division are hard, so the exact sense of who lacks means is not certain. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

54.reading: Courtesans are like the bright moon: the love that grows day by day they let waste day by day, as the moon waxes day by day and wanes day by day.
54.nuance: Each line opens with நாடொறும் நாடொறும், so the verse's own form waxes and wanes in a steady rhythm. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

claims.claim: a courtesan's love is made to wane as surely as it was made to grow

55.reading: Courtesans are like a flowering creeper in the field, humming with bees: even men without beauty, if they are not without means, they cling to and stand by as the creeper takes whatever support it finds.
55.nuance: The reading of வன்மையிலோரை and of line 2 is not certain; the sense that looks or worth do not matter, only means, is the likeliest. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

56.reading: Courtesans are like a ship that sinks in the open sea with the merchants who loaded it with fine goods: they harshly cast off those whose love for them has grown excessive.
56.nuance: The merchants have staked everything on the ship, so the image puts the ruin on the side of the most devoted. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

claims.claim: a courtesan ruins those who trust her most, as a ship drowns those who load it

57.reading: Courtesans resemble chaste wives in conduct: toward men who give them wealth enough, they serve and follow in every way.
57.nuance: The verse grants the courtesan the outward form of the பத்தினி's devotion (வழிபட்டு ஒழுகல்) and puts the whole difference in ஒத்த பொருளான், the condition of matching wealth. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

claims.claim: a courtesan's devoted service imitates the chaste wife's but follows the payment

58.reading: Flower-eyed courtesans are like a grazing beast: leaving the man whose wealth has perished, they fix their desire on another man of great wealth, as a beast whose pasture is bare moves into another's field.
58.nuance: One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

claims.claim: a courtesan leaves a man when his wealth is gone and moves to a richer one

59.reading: Courtesans are like the monkey that lives in the branches: having used up the man of little wealth, they take the man of great wealth, as a monkey leaps from branch to branch.
59.nuance: The gloss on the monkey added in 50. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

60.reading: Courtesans are like the striped-winged bee: however bright and handsome a man may be, like the red flame-of-the-forest flower, they give no thought to one without substance.
60.nuance: The bee passes over the bright முருக்கு blossom because it holds little honey, so beauty without wealth draws no courtesan. பருக்கரடு in line 2 is obscure, and the reading of 'substance' as wealth rests on the series. One of the ten glosses (51-60) on the similes the old courtesan lists in 49-50; the gloss follows her list in order. Who speaks the glosses is not stated: they describe courtesans in the third person, so they may be the poet's or the mother's continued teaching.

61.reading: Those who know call begetting children and keeping the household's dharma the chief virtue; spending one's life in pleasure with deceitful-tongued women yields nothing.
61.nuance: The verse is attributed to 'those who know' (என்ப), not to the poet. தோற்றம் ஒன்று இன்று may mean no issue at all, against the children of line 1, or simply no good result. A Jain epic by tradition here praises the householder's life, not renunciation; the fragment does not say whether a higher path was set above it.

claims.claim: begetting children and keeping household dharma is the highest virtue
a life spent in pleasure with courtesans produces nothing

62.reading: The verse calls mockery very bad and enmity very bad, even, it seems, toward those who do not bow and give, and says those who never transgress, holding these as the weightiest matters, reach the many-tiered heaven and live there.
62.nuance: Line 1's division (துனி நன்றி யார்க்கும், or துனி நன்று இயார்க்கும்) is unclear, so whether sulking is praised, blamed or left out cannot be fixed.

claims.claim: those who keep from mockery and enmity reach heaven

63.reading: If a man stands in an empty house without wealth, his women will not respect him, his great kin will shrink back at the hints of cunning men, they will all crowd off and leave, and even his own children will not cling to him.
63.nuance: வெண்டறை (bare floor) and the sense of line 2 are uncertain; line 2 also carries a repaired character.

claims.claim: without wealth a man is forsaken by wife, kin and even his children

64.reading: The poor do not speak in the assembly, the good who weigh things finely do not esteem them, and the learning the poor teach fades away dull: take this as truth.
64.nuance: The addressee, நீ in line 4, is unnamed. The failure is laid on the hearers too: even the நல்லவை, the assembly of the good, discounts the poor man.

claims.claim: poverty makes even true learning go unvalued

65.reading: Even a servant, if he has food to give, is surrounded as birds surround a fruiting tree; even the noble, once their wealth is spent, are left as birds leave a fruit tree that has fallen.
65.nuance: The two halves turn on one image, the fruit tree standing and fallen, and they reverse rank: the servant (தொழுமகன்) is courted, the noble (விழுமியர்) abandoned.

claims.claim: people gather round wealth and leave when it is gone, whatever a man's birth

66.reading: A lineage without wealth, a vow without forbearance, dharma without grace and a kingdom without ministers: the undeluded poets declare these darkness put inside darkness.
66.nuance: Each good is paired with the condition without which it fails. The verse speaks through மருள் இல் புலவர், the undeluded poets, so it presents itself as received wisdom.

claims.claim: dharma without grace, a vow without forbearance, lineage without wealth and kingship without ministers are void

67.reading: Having fallen at the feet of the hosts of sages in the Nirgrantha garb, whose faultless vision wipes away sorrow, and having done the customary courtesies, he set that story to the lute.
67.nuance: நிக்கந்த வேடம் names the Jain monks' garb outright, the clearest Jain mark in these fragments. Who the player is and what அக்கதை (that story) was belonged to the lost context; the verse survives in a commentary on the Silappathikaram.
67.event: A lute player bows at the feet of the Jain sages, pays his courtesies, and sets the story to the lute.

claims.claim: the faultless vision of the Nirgrantha sages removes sorrow

68.reading: He was a master of all ninety-six kinds of musical sequence, faultless and pre-eminent in melody and mode, and even if those who travel the sky-path were his hearers he would look at them askance and laugh harshly.
68.nuance: The editor places this after 67, but nothing shows it is the same player. The harsh laugh at even the sky-travelling beings marks a pride the verse states without judging it here.

69.reading: When the day had passed, the calves' cries and the milch cows' bells sounded, and the herdsmen's flutes of konrai pod and ambal, with the bees humming like strings, filled the air.
69.nuance: Pastoral sound is drawn as an orchestra: flutes and bees' hum as strings. The sentence is incomplete (ஆர்ப்பவும், 'and as they sounded'), and line 1's இன்று இராப்பகல் is hard to construe.

70.reading: The speaker tells his heart that the dark, oiled, flower-decked, carefully dressed hair and the rich tuft will burn in the fire of time, and asks why, even seeing them burn, it is still so bewildered.
70.nuance: Each line hands its phrase on to the next (கோலம் குயின்ற குழல், காலக் கனலெரியின்), so the verse moves step by step from adornment to the pyre. The heart has already seen the burning: its fault is not ignorance but bewilderment that survives the sight.

claims.claim: the adorned body will burn in the fire of time

71.reading: The speaker bids his heart see the glory of heads crowned with craftsmen's bright crowns come to ruin, not to be bewildered at it, to stand in the highest good path, and to be sure that if it strives there, attainment will follow.
71.nuance: சித்தி is the Jain word for the released state, and the companion of 70 moves from diagnosis to remedy; but the verse names no school and no god, so the claim is tagged general. The remedy is the heart's own effort (ஊக்கம்), with no refuge in another named.

claims.claim: one who stands in the highest path and strives will reach attainment

links.note: Both use the blind guiding the blind for a false teacher of release: the Valayapathi's அந்தகன் அந்தகற்கு ஆறு சொலல், Tirumular's குருடர்க்குக் கோல்காட்டிச் செல்லும் குருடர்.
links.teaches: Tirumular's blind guide fails for want of a true guru's sight, while the fragment names the missing thing as full knowledge in one who promises to clear past faults, so one proverb serves both a guru-centred and a knowledge-centred account of release.

gains.a: the fragment's unnamed false teacher is set beside a worked-out Saiva doctrine of the false guru, which shows how common the charge was
gains.b: Tirumular's image gains a witness outside Saivism in which the blind guide lacks knowledge that clears past deeds, not a guru's grace

links.note: Verse 49 puts the பத்தினி among the old courtesan's models; verse 57 explains that model as serving in every way those who give matching wealth.
links.teaches: Only the gloss in 57 shows why a chaste wife stands in a list of rivers, lutes and beasts: her devotion is taken over as a technique that lasts exactly as long as the payment.

links.note: Both compare a courtesan's love to a river that fails with the rain; the Naladiyar's மாரி அறவே அறுமே and வாரி அறவே அறும் lie close to the Valayapathi's lines 3 and 1.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar gives only the ending, love cut off when income ends, while the fragment makes வாரி mean both flood and income and adds the rise, so the love is shown swelling with the wealth as precisely as it dries.

gains.a: the fragment is seen reworking a known gnomic comparison, which explains its compression
gains.b: the quatrain's single pun on வாரி proves capable of a full rise-and-fall cycle the quatrain itself leaves out

links.note: The Naladiyar's wife sets her ever-renewed shyness against women who join many chests for wealth; the Valayapathi says those women serve their payers like பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர்.
links.teaches: Together they put the difference between wife and courtesan not in the service given, which the fragment says can look the same, but in what the Naladiyar's wife names: a shyness that never wears off and a bond that wealth did not buy.

gains.a: the satirical comparison gains the wife's own account of the inner thing the courtesan only imitates
gains.b: the wife's wonder is sharpened by a text conceding that the courtesan can copy the outward form of her devotion

links.note: The courtesan leaves the man whose wealth has perished for a richer one, like a beast moving to a fresh field; in 65 all followers leave a man whose wealth is spent, like birds from a fallen fruit tree.
links.teaches: Read beside 65, the courtesan's switching is not her special vice but one case of the rule the fragments state for kin and followers alike, so the satire of the courtesan rests on a general claim that people follow wealth.

links.note: Kural 60 calls good children the ornament of a home's excellence; Valayapathi 61 calls begetting children and keeping household dharma the chief virtue, and a life with deceitful women barren.
links.teaches: The fragment turns the Kural's praise of children into an argument against the courtesan: her union is measured by the household's fruit, children, and found to yield nothing.

gains.a: the fragment's verdict on the courtesan's life is grounded in the Kural's ranking of the household's goods
gains.b: the couplet's praise of children gains a counter-case showing what a life without the household's ornament is judged to lack

links.note: Kural 1047: one whose poverty has no virtue is looked on as a stranger even by his mother; Valayapathi 63: without wealth, a man's women disregard him, his kin shrink, and his own children will not cling.
links.teaches: The Kural limits its harsh rule to poverty without அறம் and names only the mother, while the fragment drops the limit and extends the desertion to wife, kin and children, which shows how far the claim reaches once its moral condition is removed.

gains.a: the fragment's sweeping claim is seen to lack the qualifying condition the Kural attaches
gains.b: the Kural's qualifier அறஞ்சாரா is shown to do real work once a version without it stands beside it

links.note: Both say the poor man's well-founded words fail: the Kural's சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும், the Valayapathi's learning that goes புல்லென்று.
links.teaches: The Kural says only that the poor man's meaning goes slack; the fragment names who lets it, the discerning assembly of the good, and carries the loss from his speech to the learning he teaches.

gains.a: the fragment's complaint is placed as a development of a known Kural rule rather than an isolated grievance
gains.b: the couplet's impersonal 'goes slack' gains named hearers, the good who weigh things, among those who discount the poor

links.note: The Naladiyar's bees do not go to the hill when the kanthal is not in flower; the Valayapathi's birds circle a fruiting tree and leave it when it falls.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar shows only the loss, that the poor have no kin, while the fragment adds the converse, a servant with food surrounded and a noble without it deserted, so the pair shows wealth outranking birth in both directions.

gains.a: the fragment's bird image is matched by the nature image an ethical anthology used for the same claim
gains.b: the quatrain's one-way rule gains its converse, that the low-born with wealth win the following the poor lose

links.note: Kural 249 likens virtue done without அருள் to a confused man seeing the truth; Valayapathi 66 lists அருள்இல் அறன் among four goods it calls darkness put inside darkness.
links.teaches: The Kural makes graceless virtue a single paradox, while the fragment sets it in a series with a vow without forbearance, a lineage without wealth and a kingdom without ministers, so grace appears as one of several enabling conditions without which a good is void.

gains.a: the fragment's one item on grace gains the Kural's fuller case for grace as the root of virtue
gains.b: the couplet's claim is shown to fit a general pattern of goods emptied by a missing condition, which the couplet alone does not show

links.note: Kural 160 ranks those who fast below those who bear harsh words; Valayapathi 66 calls a vow (நோன்பு) without forbearance (பொறைமை) darkness.
links.teaches: The Kural only ranks fasting below forbearance, but the fragment makes forbearance the condition without which a vow is worthless, a stronger claim that turns a ranking into a dependence.

gains.a: the fragment's terse item is given the Kural's reason why bearing insult is the harder discipline
gains.b: the couplet's ranking is shown being read by a later epic as a requirement rather than an order of merit

links.note: Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures tear the corpse; Valayapathi 70 says the heart, though it sees the adorned hair burn, is still bewildered.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar treats delight in adornment as ignorance that the sight of the corpse would cure, while the fragment's heart has already seen the burning and is bewildered still, so the pair separates not knowing the body's end from knowing it to no effect.

gains.a: the fragment's lament is sharpened by a verse that still trusts sight to cure desire
gains.b: the quatrain's appeal to what one has seen is shown to have a limit, a heart that sees and is unmoved

links.note: Both start from crowned kings brought to nothing and rebuke those who see it unchanged: Pattinathar's கண்டு பின்னும், the Valayapathi's கண்டால் மயங்காதே. Pattinathar's way out is reaching the feet of the Lord of the golden hall; the Valayapathi's is standing in the highest path and striving.
links.teaches: From the same sight the two draw opposed remedies, refuge at a god's feet for the Saiva poet and one's own steady effort for the fragment, which names no god; the tension holds on the reading that the fragment's ஊக்கம் is sufficient by itself.

gains.a: the fragment's call to effort stands out as godless against a Saiva poem built on the same scene
gains.b: Pattinathar's appeal to grace is shown to be one answer to a shared reproach, not the only conclusion the reproach allows

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken
music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
new_concepts.label_source: marker's label; the verses name யாழ், பண், திறம், கோவை and நரம்பு

source_issues: 49 line 1: யாறொடி, where the list of similes needs யாறொடு (river, with ...); the gloss in 51 confirms the river. Likely a misprint or a wrong division.
53 lines 2-4: the division of கரண மெனுமிலர், திரணி உபாயத்திற் றிரண்பொருள் and கரணி is doubtful, and the line-level sense cannot be fixed.
61 line 1: மக்க்ள் has a stray pulli; the word is மக்கள்.
63 line 2: repaired character (the old encoding '·' for ஃ in அஃகுப).
69 line 1: அன்றைப் பகற்கழிந் தாளின் றிராப்பகற் is hard to divide; the verse is an incomplete sentence (ஆர்ப்பவும்).

Order is the editor's. 48-66 are from புறத்திரட்டு, 67-69 from Adiyarkku Nallar's commentary on the Silappathikaram, 70-71 from the Yapparungala virutti, so the run mixes three sources and verses 67-69 need not belong together.
